In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the electric sense can encode the identity and motion of a conspecific in the presence of noise, but that motion degrades this encoding.
the primary and secondaries beats are encoded in afferents, but the motion envelope is not, except for the lower firing rate receptors.
the motion of the fish can be encoded in the spike train of electroreceptors and can be detected in the brain, but the motion can degrade the encoding of the conspecific beat frequencies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the electric fish can identify the number, identity and motion of conspecific by the beat frequencies, but the motion of conspecific can degrade the identification.
motion can be an important confound for the encoding of conspecific identity, but that the brain can use a variety of strategies to decode it.

, while fish swimming can degrade the coding of the beat frequencies, the receptors with the lowest firing rates are able to encode the low-frequency motion envelope, suggesting that the brain could use this information to identify conspecifics even in the presence of motion.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in addition to the well-known effects of active motion on the encoding of sensory information in the visual and auditory senses, motion also affects the encoding of conspecific identity in the electric sense.
the spatiotemporally complex electric signals produced by fish swimming are not necessarily a hindrance to the sensory systems that detect them.
the naturalistic signals used by electric fish to communicate can be highly complex, with the superposition of multiple beat frequencies and motion envelopes.
